title: Keeping State Across a Reload
summary: Hot reload is only useful if the game keeps its state - the player's position, the enemies, the score - while the code changes. This lesson shows the two strategies, **host-owned memory** and **save and restore**, and how to handle the hard case: a reload that changes the layout of the state itself.
markdown:
## Strategy 1: the host owns the memory

The simplest and fastest approach, popularised by Casey Muratori's *Handmade Hero*: the host allocates one big block of memory at start-up and hands it to the DLL every frame. The DLL keeps **all** of its state in that block, and none in its own globals:

```cpp-norun
struct game_memory
{
    uint64_t size;
    void*    storage;       // allocated by the host once, never freed until exit
    bool     initialised;   // false the first time
};

extern "C" __declspec(dllexport) void game_update(game_memory* memory, const game_input* input, float dt)
{
    auto* state{ static_cast<GameState*>(memory->storage) };
    if (!memory->initialised) { new (state) GameState{}; memory->initialised = true; }
    state->player.x += input->moveX * dt;
}
```

When the DLL is swapped, the block is untouched, so the new code finds the state exactly as the old code left it.

The rules that make it work:

- `GameState` is **plain data**: no virtual functions (their vptrs would point into the old DLL), no `std::string` or `std::vector` whose memory came from the old DLL's heap if it used its own CRT. Arrays with fixed sizes, plain structs, indices instead of pointers into code.
- Memory that the game needs to grow comes from a simple **arena** inside the block, not from `new`.
- No pointers to functions or string literals of the DLL are stored in the state.

## Strategy 2: save and restore

If the state has to contain richer C++ objects, the DLL can instead write its state to bytes just before it is unloaded and read it back after the new one is loaded:

```cpp-norun
// in the DLL's table
uint64_t (*save_state)(void* buffer, uint64_t capacity);   // returns bytes needed
int32_t  (*load_state)(const void* buffer, uint64_t size);
```

The host calls `save_state` on the old DLL, unloads it, loads the new one and calls `load_state`. Slower, but it handles any state, and the same code doubles as your save-game system.

## When the layout changes

Both strategies face the same hard case: you add a member to `GameState`, or change a type. The new code then reads the old bytes with the new layout, which is lesson 3.03's versioned-struct problem in another form. The same solution works:

- Put a **version number** (and size) at the start of the saved state or the memory block.
- When the new code sees an **older version**, it **migrates**: reads the old layout, fills new fields with defaults, writes the new layout.
- When it sees a version it cannot read, it **starts fresh** rather than reading garbage, and logs why.

```cpp-norun
struct StateHeader { uint32_t version; uint32_t size; };

// version 1: { int32_t x, y; }    version 2: { int32_t x, y; int32_t health; }
if (header.version == 1) { /* copy x, y; health = 100; */ }
else if (header.version == 2) { /* read as is */ }
else { /* unknown: start a new game */ }
```

Many developers simply restart when the state layout changes, and reload freely for everything else. A version number makes that decision automatic instead of a crash.

## What hot reload is good for, and what not

Excellent for: tuning movement and feel, fixing gameplay bugs while reproducing them, iterating on enemy behaviour, UI layout. Poor for: changes to data the host owns, changes to the host itself, and big structural changes, which still need a restart.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] A static variable inside the gameplay DLL
> It resets on every reload. Move it into the state.

> [!warning] Reading old state with a new layout
> Values land in the wrong fields. Version the state and migrate or start fresh.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? Which describes the host-owned-memory strategy?
- The DLL allocates its state with `new` in its own globals and gives the host a pointer to it
+ The host allocates one memory block and passes it to the DLL every frame; the DLL keeps all state as plain data in it
- The host copies the DLL's global variables into its own memory just before every reload
> Swapping the DLL leaves the block untouched, so the new code finds the state exactly as the old code left it.

? What makes state safe to keep across a reload?
- C++ objects with virtual functions, as long as they were created with `new`
- Any data, as long as it is stored in a static variable inside the DLL
+ Plain data with no pointers into the DLL, in memory the host owns
> No vptrs, no pointers to the DLL's functions or string literals, and memory from the host rather than the DLL's heap. Anything that points into the old DLL's image dangles after `FreeLibrary`, and the DLL's statics reset on every reload.

? How do you handle a change in the state's layout?
+ Store a version number and migrate older versions to the new layout
- Read the old bytes with the new layout; new fields simply start as zero
- Increase the DLL's file version so Windows converts the state
> Migration gives new fields defaults, and versions you cannot read start fresh. Reading old bytes with a new layout puts values in the wrong fields; it is lesson 3.03's versioned-struct problem again.

? Why must game state kept in host memory have no virtual functions?
- Virtual functions are too slow to call every frame
+ Each object's vptr would point into the old, unloaded DLL
- The host cannot allocate memory for objects with virtual functions
> Plain data survives the swap; code pointers, including vtables, do not.

? The state gained a new field and the new DLL finds version 1 data. What should it do?
- Read it with the new layout and carry on as usual
+ Migrate it: read the old layout, default the new field
- Crash on purpose, so the developer knows to restart
> Then write the new layout. A version number turns layout changes into a decision instead of garbage.

? Which strategy also works as a save-game system?
- Host-owned memory
+ Save and restore through `save_state` and `load_state`
- Neither; save games need a separate format
> The DLL serialises its state to bytes, which can just as well be written to a file.
```
ideas:
- Move all of your gameplay DLL's globals into a `GameState` in host memory, then reload while moving the player: the position must not jump.
- Add a `health` field, give the state a version header, and write the version-1 to version-2 migration.
